body:
Two important leaders

The Naikda rising of 1868 in the Panchmahals-Jambughoda region is particularly important because contemporary records identify its principal leaders, major locations and sequence of events.

Rup Singh Naik, also written as Rupsing or Roopsing Nayak, was associated with Dandiapur in the Panchmahals region. He had participated in an earlier period of resistance.

Joria Bhagat, also remembered as Joria Parmeshwar, was associated with Vadek, near Jambughoda. His influence rested partly on his position as a religious figure. Followers attributed extraordinary spiritual powers to him, and his religious authority helped mobilise support.

The two leaders joined forces. Contemporary accounts describe an attempt to challenge established authority and establish Naikda rule. This combined political and religious mobilisation is a defining feature of the 1868 rising.

Major events in February 1868

On 2 February 1868, Rup Singh Naik and his followers attacked the post at Rajgad in the Baria region. The rebels subsequently moved through the Panchmahals area, attacked Jambughoda and threatened Halol.

On 6 February 1868, forces associated with Joria Bhagat attacked Jetpur in the Chhota Udepur region. The confrontation encountered resistance from local state forces.

British and allied forces then organised a counteroffensive. According to the account of Narukot in the Gazetteer, an attack on the movement's centre at Vadek on 16 February 1868 dispersed its forces.

Suppression and consequences

The rebellion was defeated. Rup Singh Naik, Joria Bhagat and Galalia, identified in the Gazetteer as Rup Singh's son, were captured, tried and executed.

The immediate outcome was the destruction of the movement's organised armed resistance. British political supervision and local policing continued. The Gazetteer also records subsequent administrative measures in the Jambughoda area, reflecting the authorities' effort to reinforce control.

Suppression of an uprising should not be confused with a complete resolution of the underlying disputes. Problems concerning authority, cultivation and access to resources remained important features of the colonial eastern belt.

Why the leaders must be distinguished

Rup Singh Naik is associated especially with the movement's armed and political leadership. Joria Bhagat is remembered for the spiritual authority through which he attracted followers and participated in the challenge to colonial and princely power. Their roles were connected, but the two names do not refer to the same person.

Rup Singh Naik: Dandiapur, armed leadership, Rajgad.
Joria Bhagat: Vadek, religious mobilisation, also known as Joria Parmeshwar.
1868: Rajgad, Jambughoda, Jetpur and Vadek were significant locations.

Prelims focus

  • 1868: major Naikda rising in the Panchmahals-Jambughoda region.
  • Rup Singh Naik was associated with Dandiapur.
  • Joria Bhagat, or Joria Parmeshwar, was associated with Vadek.
  • 2 February 1868: attack on Rajgad.
  • 6 February 1868: attack on Jetpur.
  • Rup Singh Naik, Joria Bhagat and Galalia were executed after the suppression of the rising.
  • Trap: Joria Bhagat and Govind Guru were different leaders associated with different movements and periods.

[Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Rewa Kantha, ch. VII, Naikda Rising, 1868, pp. 64-65, and Narukot, History, pp. 175-176, 1880, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, address at Jambughoda concerning tribal freedom fighters, 1 November 2022, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Rup Singh Naik and Joria Bhagat: The Naikda Rising of 1868

body:
Bhil reform and resistance across the Gujarat-Rajasthan border

Tribal resistance in the wider eastern Gujarat region continued beyond the Naikda uprisings of the 19th century. One important early-20th-century example was the movement associated with Govind Guru, also known as Govindgiri.

Govind Guru worked among Bhil communities in the borderlands of present-day Rajasthan and Gujarat. His teachings encouraged social and moral reform, including abstinence from alcohol, improved community conduct and unity among followers.

He established the Samp Sabha, associated with the Bhagat movement. Sources describe its organisation in 1903. Meetings and religious gatherings helped bring followers together, while grievances against forced labour, arbitrary exactions and exploitation by local authorities gave the movement an increasingly political character.

The Mangarh event of 17 November 1913

Mangarh Hill lies in the present-day Banswara district of Rajasthan, near the Gujarat border. It is associated with Bhil communities extending into Gujarat, including the former princely territory of Sunth and adjoining regions.

On 17 November 1913, British and princely-state forces opened fire on a large gathering of Govind Guru's followers at Mangarh. The event is remembered as the Mangarh massacre.

A large number of people were killed. Published accounts and commemorative statements give different casualty figures, so an exact death toll should not be presented as securely established. The location, date, leadership and nature of the event are the essential factual distinctions.

The event shows how a social and religious reform movement could become closely connected with demands for protection from exploitative labour practices and excessive exactions. It also demonstrates that resistance in Gujarat's wider tribal belt frequently crossed the boundaries of present-day states.

Comparing the major movements

Several distinctions help explain the region's history accurately.

  • Naikda rising of 1838: connected with contested local authority, revenue collection and political intervention in eastern Gujarat.
  • Naikda resistance of 1858-1859: concentrated mainly in Panchmahals and connected with the wider unrest following 1857.
  • Naikda rising of 1868: associated with Rup Singh Naik and Joria Bhagat in the Jambughoda region.
  • Bhil Bhagat movement and Mangarh, 1913: associated with Govind Guru and the border region of Rajasthan and Gujarat.

These movements shared concerns about authority, livelihoods and exploitation, but they differed in chronology, leadership, location and immediate circumstances.

One connected view of colonial Gujarat

The economic and political changes of colonial Gujarat affected different groups in different ways. Surat lost much of its earlier maritime dominance, while Bombay became increasingly important in colonial trade. Ahmedabad's cotton mills expanded industrial production and wage employment. Cotton cultivation became more closely tied to world markets and credit. In the eastern belt, changes in revenue claims, political supervision and forest access contributed to repeated resistance.

These developments should not be reduced to a single statement that colonialism either produced progress everywhere or caused identical decline everywhere. Railways, factories and commercial agriculture created new opportunities, but their benefits were unequal. At the same time, loss of customary authority and livelihood security could generate organised opposition.

Prelims focus

  • Govind Guru, or Govindgiri, was associated with the Bhil Bhagat movement and Samp Sabha.
  • Samp Sabha is associated with 1903.
  • Mangarh massacre: 17 November 1913.
  • Mangarh Hill is in present-day Banswara district, Rajasthan, near Gujarat.
  • Naikda rising of 1868: Rup Singh Naik and Joria Bhagat.
  • Ahmedabad's first cotton mill began operating in 1861.
  • Trap: Mangarh is connected with Gujarat's tribal history, but the hill itself must not be placed inside present-day Gujarat.

[Mohanlal Sukhadia University, Folklore of Vagad, 2021, section Mangarh and Govind Giri, pp. 45-53, consulted 20 November 2026; Indian Council of Historical Research and Ministry of Culture, Dictionary of Martyrs: India's Freedom Struggle, Vol. 2, Part II, 2013, p. 241, entry Ratiyo, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, PM Attends Public Programme Mangarh Dham ki Gaurav Gatha, 1 November 2022, Background section, consulted 20 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Rewa Kantha, ch. VII, pp. 62-65, 1880, consulted 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts-III, Class 8, ch. 6, pp. 65-74; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 1, pp. 4-9.]
